utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Monday, 26th of May, 2008. Let me greet the accused, the Defence counsel, the Prosecutor and his assistants, as well as everyone assisting us in this courtroom. I'm first going to give the floor to the registrar. He has a number of IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Rebic, Adalbert. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00795; the list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 00796; the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00797; and the list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00798. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. One piece of information. Tomorrow, the Trial Chamber will issue an oral ruling regarding the guidelines, and that is following the submissions made by Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Stewart, and Mr. Khan last week. They drew the attention of the Chamber on a number of issues. In order to clarify all this, the Trial Chamber will rule tomorrow, will issue an oral ruling to clarify some of the points raised last week by the Defence counsel I've just mentioned. We could have issued this ruling today, but since it's a very significant decision, after considering the matter this morning, we decided to review the text once again, and I will read out the decision tomorrow morning because tomorrow we are sitting in the morning. This is what I wanted to tell you. We have a witness now called by Mr. Prlic. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just a clarification because on Thursday afternoon, Your Honour invited written submissions. We have prepared written submissions which subject to final checking are ready for filing. May we take it that if we do file this afternoon that could at least be -- well, potentially be helpful to Your Honours and that you would consider those written submissions before you give your ruling tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would also ask -- I would also ask that if the Trial Chamber in issuing its ruling go back to the record and see how often it gave extra time to the Prosecution on direct examination and how often Judges, in particular, Judge Prandler indicated rather robustly about the right of the Prosecution to redirect examination. Last week, what occurred in my opinion was a travesty. There was 20 minutes left on the clock. I had five minutes of redirect examination, and in my opinion, the -- what was displayed last week was not only an insensitivity to the Defence but also a display of a lack of clarity and understanding of the adversarial procedure, particularly when I'm told I can bring the witness back or I should reserve time, like a half an hour, for redirect because there's a whole host of issues why that can't happen. So I welcome Mr. Stewart's and Mr. Khan's written submissions, but again, I must say in the clearest form that I was for once in my entire career ashamed to be in a courtroom with that kind of a ruling. I had to speak with my client afterwards and reassure him that perhaps we will have better days in this court again because he was wondering how is it that Mr. Seselj is getting -- 100 per cent of his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You broached the issue, Your Honour, so I'm just responding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are reopening the discussion, but I've just told you that the Chamber will issue an oral ruling following your submissions. No need to get on your high horses and to start lecturing us. Of course, Mr. Stewart, if you want to file your written submissions, it will be a pleasure for us to read them, but in any case, the oral ruling will be handed tomorrow and will not go to the substance of these submissions. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and counsel. I think the Prosecution, we certainly recognise that it's an issue, a procedural issue of some importance to all the parties and that everyone would benefit from a swift ruling from the Trial Chamber on this point. However, if the Defence is going to be filing written submissions, I think I would, just to be careful or as a precaution, to suggest that the Prosecution may wish to be heard either in writing or perhaps to be able to at least give our position in this orally after we've read the Defence submissions. So I'm not saying that we want to file a written response. It may be that we could simply express our position on this orally after having read the Defence submissions, but in any event, Mr. President, if the Trial Chamber could keep in mind the Prosecution may wish to express its views on this matter. That's all I can say on it at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course no objections at all that the Prosecution have a right to be heard on this issue. Perhaps I could be so bold as to suggest that as the matters are not new, they have been subject to quite some submissions by my learned friend, Mr. Stewart, that perhaps the Prosecution, knowing the issue, knowing the parameters of the issue can file something also by the end of today, and Your Honours can consider both submissions prior to whatever decision you make in the next few days. If there are additional issues that arise from whatever is filed, of course Your Honours may give leave to the parties to make very short submissions on those new issues, perhaps tomorrow, but of course, Your Honour, that's a matter for you and your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would propose to file certainly by 4.00 in the normal way. I don't want to impose too much of a burden on the Prosecution, but it may be that they won't find anything especially onerous or time-consuming to respond to. Perhaps if they were to file just later today if they reasonably can, that might do the trick.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're certainly willing, Mr. President, to read the Defence submissions on this. I can consult with Mr. Scott later this afternoon, and we can see whether we can file a written response today or whether a written response is even necessary. It may be that simply we can express our views orally to the Trial Chamber and then put the position -- or put the Trial Chamber in a position to rule even more quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, since Mr. Stewart's submissions will be filed before 4.00 p.m., you will be able to read them, and by the end of the afternoon, if you wish to deal with this matter, you will be able to take the floor and talk about it. But the Chamber has considered the matter this morning and has issued a decision to clarify the guidelines, not to amend them. After reading Mr. Stewart's submissions, we'll consider whether it is necessary to amend these guidelines, but in any case, tomorrow morning we'll issue an oral ruling to clarify - let me repeat it - to clarify and not to amend the guidelines. I'm going to ask the usher to bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's happening, can I just say that we're actually going to send to Mr. Stringer, we will send our draft as it stands because subject to any possible minor tweaks, it's going to be filed very soon, so just to accelerate things, we'll send it to him straightaway. I know he's in court and got other things to do, but he and his team will have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll ask my assistant, Mr. Scott, to review that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Can you please give me your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zdravko Sancevic, born on the 20th of January, 1931.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have an occupation currently, or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am still employed as the consul general of the Republic of Croatia in our mission to Venezuela.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, have you already testified before a court about the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia, or is it the first time you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated. A few words of explanation, Witness. You have been called by the Defence of Mr. Prlic in the first stage of these proceedings. You will answer questions put to you by Mr. Prlic's counsel. After that, the other Defence counsel may, if they wish to do so, put questions to you. Then the Prosecution as part of the cross-examination will put questions to you. The four Judges sitting before you may also ask questions. After the Prosecution, the Defence, if it still has some time available, will put questions to you as part of the re-examination. According to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, every hour and a half we have a break, a 20-minute break, but if at any time you feel unwell, if for some reason you want us to adjourn briefly, please ask us to do so. Having said that, I'm now going to give the floor to Mr. Prlic's counsel. He's going to put a number of questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone in and around the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Sancevic, I understand you served as an ambassador. You're currently have an ambassadorial function. It's my understanding you wish to be addressed as Ambassador Sancevic; is that correct? You're going to have to speak up because we have to make a record. You don't have to lean forward, but if you speak up, we'll pick it up.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You don't have to shout. The mics are pretty good, but -- as I also understand, I heard this coming on the way to the court, that you've had some heart problems and some health problems, and so if you do feel like it's -- this is too stressful, let us know we'll take a break, okay?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. With the Court's leave and unless there are any objections from the Prosecution, I'm going to briefly touch on your background, and I'm going to ask for you to verify it. As I understand, you were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1931?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That you left around -- 1944 to 1945, you left Bosnia-Herzegovina for Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You and your family moved to Venezuela in 1948; your father had some sort of a business, a lumber business, wood-cutting business, and after the war, everyone moved to Venezuela; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I also understand that you have been educated and received a doctorate in, I guess, petroleum engineering, having first received -- having first received your undergraduate and graduate education in the United States.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: My Ph.D is not from the United States. It is from Venezuela.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But your bachelor's and your masters are from -- what is it, the University of Colorado? Is that the mining and ...

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: No. It is the Colorado School of Mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Now, as I understand it, from 1953 to 1961-62 you worked as an engineer for Shell Oil Company.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you held other jobs in the oil industry until you retired somewhere around 1990, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have been retired as of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you've also taught at the university over there in Caracas as I understand it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I think that's enough of your background prior to the events in Croatia, but as I understand it, in 1990 or 1991, you went to Croatia as a volunteer - I think it was 1991 - as a volunteer to fight in the Croatian Home Guard once Croatia came under attack by the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thereafter, you briefly worked with or you were assigned to, I believe, the Ministry of Information?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Not to the -- to the Ministry of the Interior but to the Ministry of Information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then you were, for a short period, I believe, for about a year, you were the Minister Of Emigration as opposed to immigration, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was during the coalition government of the democratic union throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And thereafter, you were -- as I understand it, you were appointed towards the end of 1992 as Croatia's ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you stayed in that position until about what, 1995, was it or 1996?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Early 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thereafter, you served, I believe, in the Samobor, and you held one seat in the parliament, a seat that's normally designated to Croats from the diaspora?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I also failed to mention that at some point, you also worked as the president of the board of directors of the Zagreb University, and that was, I believe, in 1992 to 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That was the Administrative Council of the Zagreb University.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was that about just very briefly; could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: In English, [In English] it was the president of the board of trustees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, all right. For those of us who don't know what the board of trustees does, could you just tell us in a few words?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In western universities - because at that time there were also eastern universities - in western universities, frequently, in particular in the United States, there is a board of trustees comprising gentlemen elected to oversee the work of the university. They draft plans for its activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it one of the reasons that you were part of that board was because you had been a professor in Caracas?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, except for being a professor, I was a director of the School Of Oil Engineering at the Central University in Caracas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, let's go right into 1991 when you first arrived. Could you please tell us, what did you do with the Home Guard when you first came to Croatia and volunteered?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived as a volunteer, I registered myself, and I was a private. I was with the National Guards for four months. Once the four-month period ended, I was appointed minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You were appointed minister. What -- minister to where? Is that when you were appointed Minister Of Immigration?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed Minister for Emigration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Emigration, sorry. Now, as I understand it -- during that four-month period while you are with the Home Guard, you were also doing some work with the Ministry of Information. Could you please tell us exactly what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: When I was seconded by the Home Guards to the Ministry of Information, I had to organise within the ministry a mechanism to receive information in Europe, since all news agencies had been left behind in Belgrade. They had their seat there. In a way, I had to keep the Croatian government and president informed of the events that took place in Europe the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, sir. If I understand it correctly, primarily your job was to gather the news information, condense it so Dr. Tudjman, the then president, could have it every morning. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, it did not only concern news information. It also involved television, radio, and all sorts of information one could gather through the day concerning Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again, why didn't Dr. Tudjman just turn on the radio or the television or pick up a newspaper to find out?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe he wanted to have it in writing. At least that's what I was told. He wanted to have a brief of at least one and a half pages of the recent news in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you went to the Ministry of Emigration, how was it that you were appointed? I mean, you went to being a retired doctor in petroleum engineering to a volunteer private, and now you're all of a sudden you're a Minister of Emigration. How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Truth be said, I don't know where it came from. But in any case, and as far as I could learn, President Tudjman had read a book which had been written by my father. The book is called "From the Bosnian Forests to Venezuela," since he was involved in forestry and lumber as an industrialist. Upon reading that book, as he said once, he arrived at a conclusion that I was a member of a family which before the war had been well-known and esteemed in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. How is it that your father picked Venezuela, incidentally?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a group of industrialists in Italy right after the war who were involved in forest -- the forest business from the then-Yugoslavia. They were there awaiting free elections in Yugoslavia. However, after almost three years of waiting, they never saw such elections, upon which that group of people decided to go somewhere. The first option they had was Ethiopia. However, Mr. Negus did not contribute his own share in the general capital, and the whole idea fell through. Something else had to be devised. The then Venezuelan minister Henrique Tejeva Paris came and convinced my father to depart for Venezuela.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, getting back to the Ministry of Emigration, could you please tell us exactly -- well, first of all, when you were appointed on or about, and for how long did you serve?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of December 1991 was when I was appointed. I took the oath a few days later in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, so sorry. In the transcript, just a point of clarification. On page 12, line 22, in the English text, I can see "Mr. Negus [French spoken]." Is this the emperor of Ethiopia, the Negus, or is it somebody else?" Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, His Honour is asking you a question. When they ask questions, you know, you need to answer them.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Of course, yes, I didn't understand. I didn't hear you too good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question had to do with going back when your father was planning on going to Ethiopia, and you mentioned a particular minister, I believe, or a Mr. Negus. Who was that individual?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Negus was the head of the state of Ethiopia. He was the Ethiopian emperor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I continue? All right. There's no drama here. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to be on the safe side, your father was not running away from the authorities, you know, because of any particular affiliation during World War II, and by that I mean having fought on the other side, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: He was on the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And what side was that, just to be ...

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: You know when somebody -- well, when -- my father was of Jewish origin, and that fact alone meant that he was on the right side with the allies. For example, my father's lawyer was a member of the royal government in London. His name was Miro Shulte [phoen], and later on he was a member of the government that was popularly known as Tito's Subasic government. What else can I tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think that's enough because it's sort of a -- it's extra material that we can dispose with for the moment. But getting back to the Ministry of Emigration, what exactly did this ministry do in general terms?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I had to draft a plan of my future work because that ministry did not exist before, and its main task was concerned with the possibility that a certain number of people who resided outside of Croatia wanted to return to Croatia. The first task was to establish how many such immigrants there were because there were all sorts of immigrants. There are those who left Croatia in the 17th century, and there is also those who left in the 19th and 20th century and so on and so forth. In other words, we had to define primarily who the Croatian immigrants were, and after that we had to see how to facilitate their return to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now let me interrupt you here. Did that also include, for instance, Croats who were living in, say, Bosnia-Herzegovina or any of the republics within the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, generally speaking, but this also included citizens who were not Croats who had left Croatia and were considered Croatian emigrants. First of all, we had to define the term "emigrant," and we did. An emigrant is a person who permanently resides outside of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now as I understand it, you were there from early December 1991 until August 1992, correct, in that position?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during that period, did you have an opportunity to be at any meetings hosted by President Tudjman where he presided over?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was present at several VONS meetings. The abbreviation stands for the Council for Security and Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, and that's V-O-N-S, right? You're shaking your head. We need to make a record.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, yes. I was present at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in August -- sometime in August 1992, you were appointed ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How was it, to your understanding, that you were selected for that position?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: When that government stepped down and towards the end of my term as Minister of Emigration, President Tudjman approached me and suggested that I should be good for that position. This was on the very eve of the proclamation of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He himself told me that that decision was based on the reputation of my father, the reputation that my father enjoyed in Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war. My father was a businessman, and as such he was well loved by people in Bosnia and Herzegovina because he was very tolerant and all ethnic groups and religious groups found it easy to accept him. He helped all the religions, actually four of them: the Catholics; the Islam; the Serbian orthodox church; and the Jewish religion, i.e., the Jewish community in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where did your father come from exactly? Was it in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: He was born on Mount Kozara, which was a place famous for rebels during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you -- let me just break it down. Was he Herzegovinian, or was he from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: He was from Bosna Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So he was not Herzegovinian?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when did you actually take up your position as ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was appointed, if my memory serves me well, sometime around the 14th of October or thereabouts, and I handed my credentials to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic on the 18th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could just very briefly -- I'll show you a couple of documents. I don't know if Madam Usher has presented you with our binders with your documents there.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could look at 1D 02926. 1D 02926.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you recognise this document and if so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: These are my credentials that I handed Mr. Alija Izetbegovic on behalf of my president, Dr. Franjo Tudjman. This is a copy of my formal credentials appointing me ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: A plenipotentiary and the first in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was my next question. At that time when you were appointed, and actually when you presented your documents, your credentials, I should say, to the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were there any other ambassadors serving in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I was the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we see that -- you tell us that sometime in August was when you were appointed, and it's not until the 18th of December, you say, that you were actually presented your credentials. Could you please tell us what took so long?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: No. In August, I was no longer the Minister of Emigration, and the procedure was as follows: First, the Independent Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established, and the process lasted -- actually, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina became independent on either the 1st or the 2nd -- actually it was on the 2nd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 2nd, which month?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Sancevic, the question I had asked you is what took you so long, and now you said that Bosnia and Herzegovina became independent on either the 1st or the 2nd, but which month?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I didn't say the month. In the month of March. In the third month of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, please tell us. When you got to Bosnia, where did you set up the embassy of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Sarajevo and when I handed my credentials, I talked to Mr. Izetbegovic about the setting up of the embassy, and his advice to me was not to set it up because it would be destroyed the following day by the great Serbian forces around Sarajevo, so he recommended that I should go somewhere else and set up my embassy somewhere else. He suggested Zenica is a good place. But I decided to set up my seat in Neum and to commute, so I became a commuting ambassador or a roaming ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us exactly how long did that last, how long were you in Neum, and while you were this roaming ambassador, what exactly you did and what functions the embassy carried out?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever. My first task was to learn a few things about Bosnia and Herzegovina since I had not been familiar with Bosnia and Herzegovina or at least not enough because I had left Bosnia and Herzegovina as a child. So I did not have any other functions save for learning and getting to know Bosnia and Herzegovina during that period of time, which coincided with the first half of the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What exactly did you do as the roving ambassador? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not roam that much, but my idea was definitely to get to learn Bosnia and Herzegovina. I made three journeys. Actually, there were three directions that I could take on my travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which directions were they? And this would have been in 1993, right, not 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1993. One direction was towards Tomislavgrad, another one towards Livno. Actually, that was still the first direction. The second direction was -- let me try and remember. It was in the direction of Prozor and Central Bosnia. And the third direction was mostly along the course of the Neretva River and the beginning of the flow of the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about up in the Posavina? Did you go towards that direction at all?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I did. I went there, as well, but I did not enter the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina because it was impossible because that area at the time had been captured by the great Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was the purpose for these trips? Who was -- what would you do?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I mostly spoke to the local authorities there, to the mayors, the heads of municipalities, in order to get a feeling for everything that was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. Witness, you have said on line 14, page 19, that you could not enter the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I find that a bit surprising. Did you not come from that territory? Neum was in the territory and Tomislavgrad and the Posavina also. Did you mean that you could not enter the Posavina because the Serbs prevented you from that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. Access to the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was from the south-west, from the territory of southern Croatia, whereas access from the north was impossible because that was under the control of the great Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you said that you met with the officials in those places and were trying to gather some information. What did you do with that information, if anything?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: This information served for my own personal planning and had to do with what I would be doing in the future and where I would be setting up my embassy; and the second purpose was to get familiar with the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina because I was a rookie there, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you sending reports to the Minister of Foreign Affairs or beyond that at that point?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I sent very short reports with the same contents to the Minister of Foreign Affairs and to President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. How were you sending this information? Were you typing it up on a computer, e-mailing it? Were you faxing it? What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I didn't have any of that at the time. I would put together very brief letters containing a few sentences, and I would send them either via courier or whether -- I would take those letters to Zagreb myself whenever I went there. And then I would also have an opportunity to discuss the letter with the Minister of Foreign Affairs and President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long were you in this capacity as a roving ambassador, so to speak, and how long did you stay in Neum before you moved on to the next spot to set up the embassy for Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to say that in Neum, I lived within the circle of the Mostar University, and all that lasted up to August 1993 when I set up my embassy in Medjurgorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why pick Medjurgorje in August of 1993? Why not move to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already told you, President Izetbegovic himself told me to postpone my arrival in Sarajevo because I was under siege, and if I had decided to set up the embassy there, it would have been destroyed by the greater Serbian forces according to President Tudjman himself --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic, the interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- and why I chose Medjurgorje -- it was convenient because the area was rather calm. You know that Medjurgorje is a sacred place among the Catholic population and that there's no fighting in the area. On the other hand, a lot of different visitors had to pass through Medjurgorje on route to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and a majority if not humanitarian convoys en route to Bosnia and Herzegovina passed through Medjurgorje as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I understand what you're telling us here is that the border -- the Croatian border, the border for the Republic of Croatia was nearby. Is that what you're attempting to say, that Medjurgorje was near there and that's why -- one of the reasons that you selected it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the important thing was the fact that most of the humanitarian aid from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina passed through there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to draw your attention to the fact that your last question was a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you're aware of it, and you want to avoid that yourself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I was trying to add some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during this -- before we go into what exactly you were doing in Medjurgorje -- well, let me just go back to what was just touched upon. From Medjurgorje to the border of the Republic of Croatia, what's the distance, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the exact number of kilometres, but I suppose we are talking about 25 to 30 kilometres or a few more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before we talk about what you did there, could you tell us whether you were venturing into Sarajevo at all during this period?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I went to Sarajevo after having handed my credentials on two occasions, during the second half of 1992 and early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was the purpose for those visits?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: My main duty was to maintain contacts with the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which were in Sarajevo; however, there were periods when the Bosnian-Herzegovinian authorities were in Zagreb, and that's where I would -- when I would go to Zagreb to meet with various ministers and officials of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's talk about your activities in Medjurgorje. Please, first of all, tell us what sort of services did the embassy of the Republic of Croatia provide at that location, and we're talking now August 1993 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, at that location, I performed a lot of consular services such as issuing certificates, visas, certificates of nationality, passports. In other words, whatever one should expect from an embassy with a good consular service. This is as far as Medjurgorje is concerned, and I have also told you that the political relationship with the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was something that was maintained either in Sarajevo when I went there or when I came closer to Zagreb where the officials of Bosnia and Herzegovina were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. How large of a staff did you have?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, there were four individuals, and then the numbers steeply shot to some 15 staff, but I can't be pinned down to give you the exact figure. At any rate, between several individuals until ultimately 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how long was the embassy for the Republic of Croatia in Medjurgorje? How long was it there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Until the Washington Agreement was signed. As soon as it was signed, I started relocating the embassy to Sarajevo. The process of relocation lasted from March to the end of April, possibly early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, before we talk about citizenships and passports and maybe even visas, I want to touch upon what you said, that you were issuing certificates, this concept.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mean certificates?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's how it's -- it's translated as certificates in English, but I know it from you to be potvrda. I'm having a tough time with it --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is right. Potvrda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Normally I'm fluent in everything else.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: This was a piece of paper we issued to individuals to enable them to go to Croatia. Now, there were many reasons why individuals wanted to go to Croatia. For instance, there were individuals who had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. We're going to go step by step. Who -- when you say "individuals," who are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Of those who had interests that were out of the ordinary to enter Croatia or to traverse Croatia regardless of their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, was this some sort of -- what did one have to show or do in order to get this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the individual's identity had to be verified. You cannot issue an individual with a document before you have ascertained his or her identity, which meant that the individual had to bring a number of documents to the embassy on the basis of which their identity could be ascertained and the document, the requested document issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What sort of documents would they need to present?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Primarily identity cards. There were cases where identity cards had burned, and so on, so forth. If they didn't have an identity card on them, then they had to have some sort of a document with their photograph. If there was none of that to be produced, either, they had to present us with a birth certificate or a marriage certificate or any other sort of document that could serve to identify the person concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What if the person had no documents at all?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Then the person would not be issued by -- with a certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what was the purpose for issuing these certificates?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: You see, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, though there were admittedly borders between the two countries, ever since the Turkish Empire left the area, ever since 1878, there had not been firm borders, as it were, between the two countries. All of a sudden, a border emerged between the two, and business had to be taken care of, which was the sort of business that is normally carried out between two states that had recognised one another. Order had to be introduced, some sort of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And for -- with these documents, how long could someone go into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: We were quite liberal in that regard. I remember that we were developing the procedure over a period, but normally the approach was of a case-to-case basis. If somebody wanted to cross Croatia in order to join their family in France, then we would give them a longer period of time. Now, if someone wanted to cross into Croatia in order to visit their family or to visit someone who was wounded and was hospitalised, we would give documents on shorter periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there are questions -- I will -- no questions, okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's talk about those who wanted to have a passport. What was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where the individual concerned had a Bosnian passport, we would issue him or her with a visa that would be placed on the passport. Visas could not be issued in cases where the individual did not have a passport. In general, one could apply for Croatian citizenship through our embassy, but the application was forwarded to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Croatia, the reason being the law on citizenship, which was already in force by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's talk about that law, then. If we go to 1D 02918. 1D 02918. Have you found it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Was this the document -- did you use this document at any point in time back then when you were the ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina in Medjurgorje?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the date of the promulgation of the law, the 28th of June, 1991, so ever since it had been issued, I applied it in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And was it this law that you applied when somebody came and wanted to get Croatian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I understood your testimony earlier, and I don't intend to lead you, but it was -- you needed citizenship before you could qualify for a passport? If I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if somebody already could establish that he had Croatian citizenship, then it was just a formality for you to issue a passport, whereas if there was no evidence of somebody being or having Croatian citizenship, they had to go first establish that, and then the passport would be issued.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: The applicants for a passport had to have either a certificate of their citizenship -- or rather, any sort of certificate which proved that they were citizens of that country, or they had to have a document called domovnica, which is the certificate of Croatian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's the specific document that they need to show?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's just take a hypothetical. An individual from Bosnia-Herzegovina arrives in Medjurgorje and wishes to establish or to get Croatian citizenship. Could you walk us through the procedure step by step? It doesn't matter whether they are a Croat, a Serb, or a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Nowhere in the law is an individual's ethnicity mentioned. Any person could apply for citizenship, according to this law. The procedure for applying for citizenship was one's origin, one's birth on the territory of the Republic of Croatia; naturalization; and by application of international treaties. Furthermore, other documents were required, and in addition to the ones I mentioned which were required for the verification of an individual's identity, we asked them to produce some other documents. If the person concerned met all the requirements, he or she could apply for Croatian citizenship. The basic article of the law prescribing the requirements for citizenship of Croatia is Article 8, naturalization. That article clearly specifies the procedure according to which one could apply for and be granted citizenship. Where an individual was unable to meet all the requirements under Article 8, there were other articles, such as Article 9, Article 16, and so on and so forth, which I can explain to you if you wish me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just give us a very brief explanation so we know.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: About these articles, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, in particular you said Article 8, and then I believe Article 16 is also relevant because it makes reference to Article 8.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Articles 9 and 16 refer back to Article 8: Where an individual could not be granted citizenship under Article 8, he or she was able to apply for citizenship under Articles 11 and 16. Article 11 relates to emigrants, to emigrants or emigres and their descendants. According to this law, they could be granted citizenship without any restrictions in term of their blood lineage. In other words, an emigre or emigrant could have been away from the country for 100 years through his ancestors and could still be granted citizenship under Article 11. Now, Article 16 also relates to the Croats residing outside of Croatia but who are not emigrants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we have a few moments before we take our break, and before we go into the issuance of passports and what have you, I just wanted to ask you whether you were familiar at all with the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation between the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That was the fundamental agreement which was law to me. You know that agreements between two countries takes supremacy in relation to all the other laws of the country; therefore, the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation between Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia was considered law, in my view, all the way until the Washington Agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at P 00339. P 00339. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can see that this document was generated or the agreement was generated on July 21, 1992, and as I understand it based on your testimony, you would have been with the Ministry of Emigration at that time, July 21, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: No. This followed my term of office in the Ministry of Emigration. The Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation between the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia was, as we can see, signed in the month of June, namely on the 21st of June, 1992 -- you are right. I'm sorry. I have to withdraw what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That's okay. If you can just look at paragraph number 7.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here, we see here "the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia will reciprocally allow their citizens to acquire dual citizenship."

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, am I to understand that somebody from Bosnia and Herzegovina who had citizenship in Bosnia and Herzegovina could also have obtained Croatian citizenship based on this Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Let me just indicate that I have dual citizenship but not that of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia; rather, of Venezuela and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And as I understand it, this is the law that you are applying with respect to those who wanted to get dual citizenship at the time, the one that we've been discussing, this law on Croatian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, once somebody has their paperwork all filled out, is it up to you to make that decision? Are you the one that decides who will or will not get citizenship? Or is that decision made somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: The decision was taken by the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was that -- did the Ministry of the Interior have an office there in Medjurgorje, or did you have to send the documents to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: We had to send the documents to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what kind of a time frame are we talking about? How long would it take the Ministry of Information to get back to you -- the Ministry of the Interior to get back to you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: You see, it varied. At times, they would take a bit longer because they had to go through the identity checks themselves to ascertain the identities of the persons involved. It could take anything between a couple of weeks to a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Once somebody was approved, what would be the next step?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next step normally was that the person involved would apply for a passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what would be the procedure for obtaining a passport, assuming that the individual got his citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: The procedure was far simpler because it only required photographs and a document of citizenship and/or domovnica, rather, the official certificate of the citizenship; and of course, there were forms to be filled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just a couple of follow-ups to make sure we have this on the record. If you could look at 1D 02919. Do you have it, sir? 2919. And then we're going to discuss 2920. All right. If you could look at these two documents, starting with 2919. We see that this is a correction to the Law on Croatian Citizenship. Were you aware of this correction and, if so, to what extent if any did it affect -- did it impact on the law that you had been applying?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Not much. These were amendments to legislation, and we have quite a few of those passed nowadays. This is the normal procedure, and the amendment we see here was not that significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would that be the same for the next document, 1D 02920?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, if you could look at that. This is an amendment to the Law on Croatian Citizenship.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The amendment relates to children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: How a child born abroad can acquire citizenship through its -- or rather, the child's origins. If I may be allowed to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You have a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian law is quite liberal in some aspects. Why? Because almost the same numbers of Croats reside abroad as can be found in Croatia. I'm speaking of some 4.5 million or thereabouts. For this reason, the intention was to simplify the procedure for the acquiring of citizenship for children born abroad, and it states here specifically, citizenship can be obtained through one's background. When we were speaking of the ways in which one could acquire Croatian citizenship earlier on, we did mention that one could become a citizen of Croatia, a national of Croatia through personal background and provenance, and this is how it came to be formulated in the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think this would be a good time to take the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, Mr. Ambassador, before we move on, going back to -- I had asked a question, and I'm not sure whether we're clear on this, and that was with respect to giving Croatian citizenship to anyone who came from the former Yugoslavia, and I wasn't clear whether -- well, my question wasn't that clear, but I want to -- I want you to focus on Article 11 going back to document 1D 02918, 2918. This is the Law on Croatian Citizenship. Perhaps you could look at the last paragraph within Article 3, and I'll read it slowly. It says, "In the sense of paragraph 1 of this Article, an immigrant is a person who immigrated from Croatia with the intention to live permanently abroad." Would this definition apply to Croats who had immigrated to Bosnia-Herzegovina, keeping in mind, now, that you have two separate countries?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Could you please repeat -- [Interpretation] please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We talked a little about who is an immigrant, and you indicated that those Croats who lived abroad, for one reason or another they had immigrated to either get away from Tito, for instance, or to look for work or had left even well before the, you know -- it could be two or three generations, whatever the case. I had asked a question about whether that definition applied to Croats living in the former republics of Yugoslavia, keeping in mind now that Yugoslavia has disintegrated; you have various different countries, Bosnia-Herzegovina being one of them. So would a Croat who was born in Croatia but now was living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, would he be considered an immigrant within this definition?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: No. In the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this article was not applicable, this being Article 11 concerning emigres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said something about visas. And my question now is, did you -- when you were ambassador there in Medjurgorje, were you involved in issuing what has been termed in this courtroom as transit visas, for people to transit through Croatia to go to third countries, to go beyond Croatia? Was that part of your mandate?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how would one qualify for such a transit visa? Because you indicated before that one could be -- somebody could be issued a certificate, a potvrda, and with that they could enter Croatia to do whatever business, visit family, go to the hospital, or whatever. So now the question is, did somebody else -- why would they need a transit visa and not one of those certificates?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: A transit visa could be issued only alongside a passport. There were passports of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of the Republic of Croatia, and of various other nations, in cases of UNPROFOR personnel and in the cases of humanitarian assistance and so on and so forth. For example, at a certain moment, the State of Israel forwarded a number of passports, against which we issued visas to those who were supposed to transit Croatia on their way to Israel. It is a geographical problem. When one looks at Bosnia-Herzegovina being surrounded on three sides by the Republic of Croatia, then of course the issue of transit visas becomes pertinent because they needed such visas in order to go further afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there are any questions on these issues, I'm going to move on to another topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if you look at the transcript, page 34, line 2, if I understand correctly, you stated that nationals from Bosnia and Herzegovina did not come under Article 11 of the law we are currently reviewing, the Law on Croatian Citizenship. Can you explain why this law does not apply to them? Because Bosnia and Herzegovina is a country distinct from Croatia, so I do not understand why the law does not apply to the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not that it did not apply to the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was necessary for a person who had emigrated, that that person had emigrated from the area of the then-state of Croatia. As you know, during the Austro-Hungarian empire, there was the Kingdom of Croatia, Dalmatia, and Slavonia. If someone moved out of the eastern part of that kingdom while it was still a Croatian state, then that person could be given the status of an emigrant. It is necessary for such a person to move out of there territory of Croatia, which covered a certain territory at that particular time. The territory occupied by the Croatian state changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that question, we know that in Bosnia, you had three constituent nations, Croat being one of them. You had the Muslim nation; you had the Serb nation; you had the Croatian nation. So based on the question that was just posed to you, would Croats who were indigenous to Bosnia and Herzegovina, would they have been considered to have immigrated to that -- to Bosnia and Herzegovina from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think we considered such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, still on the same subject. Witness, it is not quite clear to me what it means that Croatians in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not considered after the country had become independent as emigrants. Does it mean that the rule of Article 16 did not apply to them, or what was the effect of this denial of the status of emigrant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could ask and receive it under a different Article rather than the Article concerning emigrants, that is, Article 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And which article would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Article 16, which refers to the -- which refers to the foreigners who are asking for Croatian citizenship and don't qualify as emigrants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And could you, then, point out to the Bench which Article applied to those who were considered emigrants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 11. It refers to emigrants. In that Article, there is a definition of what or who an emigrant is. It is a person who permanently resides abroad and had left the territory of the Croatian state as it was at that particular time. The territory changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I ought to have found out myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to switch topics now, and as I understand it, during this period while you were serving in the various capacities, Ministry of Emigration and then as ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina, you participated or sat in various meetings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to document P 02088, 2088. We`ve seen this document before in this courtroom. It's dated April 24, 1993. If you look at the first paragraph, or the preamble, you could call it, we see your name, Ambassador Zdravko Sancevic. Do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you present when this joint statement was issued by the two signatories, which is Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic, witnessed by President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, look at -- just a couple of points -- with respect to this joint statement, we see in paragraph 1 that there was a meeting on March 3, 1993, in New York, and it talks about the six members of the coordination body. Then it talks about the work on the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan to the extent possible considering the character of the provisions and present circumstances. Now, my question is, were you familiar with the contents of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 4, again, I just need a verification. Paragraph number 4, I don't read the whole part of it, but it talks about achievements of political goals and it says, "i.e., the independence and territorial integrity of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the framework of the Vance-Owen Plan accepted and signed by the signatories of the statement and success in the fight against the aggressor who wants to break the state apart, occupy its territory, and annex the occupied territories to Greater Serbia." Sir, was that your understanding that part of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan called for the independence and territorial integrity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within a certain framework?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. President, I object to the question as leading. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could ask for a ruling before the witness answers, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was your understanding of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan? Do you recollect, what was your understanding of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan? What did it call for?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Peace Plan was presented in early 1993. It is a plan following the line of thinking of Mr. Ahtisaari, who was appearing on behalf of the European union with the task of studying different possible ways of the internal arrangement of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After having studied - that is, Mr. Ahtisaari and his commission - after having studied the unitary state and then the possibility of a loose federation or a confederation, they arrived at certain conclusions. The idea of a federal state was adopted as regards Bosnia-Herzegovina. The plans such as Cutileiro's and then Vance-Owen's were based, for the most part, on Ahtisaari's selection, which stated that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be arranged on a federal basis, irrespective of whether it will be divided into cantons, provinces, or any others, but the bottom line was a federal state, and the Vance-Owen Plan was based on the notion of federalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we know that there was a major event in Medjurgorje on May 18, 1993. May 18, 1993. That would have been the period, based on your previous testimony, where you would have been in Neum, headquartered in Neum while you were roving or acting as a roving ambassador. My first question is, were you by any chance at the meeting that was held on May 18, 1993, in Medjurgorje?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. That meeting was a result of President Tudjman's initiative for peace. It comprised two parts. The first one was a meeting of President Tudjman on the same day in Split, the 18th, with the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. -- I cannot recall the name right now. He was a minister of the Russian Federation. Then, there was to be a meeting with Mr. Petersen, a Dane, who was presiding -- or rather, whose country was presiding the EU at the time. Lord Owen was to be included as well as Mr. Stoltenberg, I believe, although I'm not completely certain about him. In any case, I saw Lord Owen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. What happened first at the meeting in Split before the second meeting in Medjurgorje on the 18th of May, if you recall? And I'm assuming that you were present at the time; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I was present at all talks of President Tudjman with these VIP personalities, these world figures of -- these figures of the world politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What were the discussions about in Split?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: The discussions were about how to achieve peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was anything concrete resolved? I mean, there's a lot of talking going on during this period, but was anything concretely resolved at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the meeting which happened in the afternoon of that same day in Medjurgorje, it was determined that the Vance-Owen Plan should not be abandoned altogether. It was also arranged that there should be an agreement on the most important steps to be taken with regards to the Vance-Owen Plan, i.e., how to organise these initial provinces of the Vance-Owen Plan. How, and in what ways will people of different nations take part in the provincial life and to elect a prime minister. Mr. Jadranko Prlic was elected as the prime minister. He was -- I was present when he was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you here for a second, and let's look at document 1D 0 -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. Before we leave the previous document, I would like to have -- to put a question to the witness regarding the same paragraph 4 that we have spoken about. In that paragraph, we find on the third line from the bottom in the English version, it speaks of the Vance-Owen Plan, "accepted and signed by the signatories of this statement ..." which would be Izetbegovic and Mate Boban. Do you have any commentary on this reference to accepted and signed by both signatories? Does it mean that there was an equal attitude of all those present vis-a-vis the VOPP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is document P 02088.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I was present there, I could see that after this Split agreement, there was a lot of effort that was being put in. Mr. Petersen was present there on behalf of the EU; Lord Owen was there, as well, and it is there that the participants, Mr. Izetbegovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you here, Ambassador Sancevic. The question from His Honour was about the previous document, not the one that I was questioning you on or was about to question you on but on the document of P 02088. This is the joint statement, and it's April 24, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is also on the screen in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Well ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it. It is a -- the joint statement of document 2088.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: His Honour's question was in regards to paragraph number 4, so it's about this document, not about the meeting in Split. This would have been on May 18th. So if you could answer His Honour's question on that particular day. I'm just trying to be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's much appreciated, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to jog my memory a bit as regards Article 4. I read it. It is de facto what is contained in the document. In other words, that the signatories wish to stress that the conflict between the units of the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina are contrary to the policy represented by the representatives of the two peoples. That is the gist of the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: My question was much narrower. It refers to the line which mentions the Vance-Owen Plan and comments, I quote, "... accepted and signed by the signatories of this statement ..." Should this -- does this mean, can we take from this that both the Croat and the Bosnian-Herzegovinian side had what attitude? The same attitude towards the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not insist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if you're not satisfied with the answer, Your Honour -- let me ask -- I'll ask the follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It says that both of them signed on the basis that they had agreed. To your understanding, to your understanding, you being there, had the President of the Presidency Alija Izetbegovic, had he accepted the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and that it should be implemented based -- was that your understanding, or was there some other understanding?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: No. At that time, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic agreed on unreservedly to sign the declaration as well as the Vance-Owen Plan. At that time, he accepted the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. If we could go to 1D 01595. 1D 01595. Now, before we had gone back to this previous document, we were talking about May 18, and this document appears to be the minutes of the meeting in Medjurgorje, and you did touch upon your understanding of the meeting. I would like to focus your attention to item number 3. We've seen this document before. We don't need to go through it in great detail, but item number three says, "The president of the transition of government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be Jadranko Prlic. In agreement with the Muslim side, he shall recommend a balanced government of eight ministerial portfolios of which three shall remain without appointment. In case an agreement is impossible to reach, he shall consult with the co-chairmen of the peace conference." Ambassador Sancevic, when you indicated before that Dr. Jadranko Prlic had been appointed as - I believe you called him prime minister; I think that's what you indicated - this is what you meant, correct? That he was appointed at that time or accepted by both sides as the President of the transitional government for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Pardon me. I don't remember having said minister or prime minister. I wanted to say the prime minister, premier, the president of the government, if you wish. Mr. Jadranko Prlic was not present, but all those who were accepted Jadranko Prlic with enthusiasm, I dare say, because they considered him to be the most appropriate person for the job. There were people there who did not have much to do with the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but together with those who were present there, they agreed upon that appointment including those who were directly involved in the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. I dare say he was the star at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 02404, 2404.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before, and can you tell us -- or the contents of it, and can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the famous Medjurgorje agreement signed on the 18th of May in the evening or at night. I was present there, and I was impressed with the conclusions reached. It was agreed upon that Mr. Prlic be the prime minister. That was number one. Number two, it was agreed that a temporary or interim provincial government be appointed for Mostar, Travnik, and Zenica. Also, the proportion of Muslims and Croats in that government was agreed upon. Another thing that impressed me was the appointment of an interim public ombudsman, and a coordination body was agreed upon as well as the central government, then the military agreement, and that all those who are detained be released. De facto, it meant that the prisons that existed on both sides were to be shut down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And we can see from the very first paragraph that this is -- this was at Hina News Agency that had received this particular text. From you familiar with Hina, the Hina News Agency?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
