utterances.text: All right. So can we conclude from this that this was also announced publicly, this agreement, so that the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina could see for themselves ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I object to the form of the question. He can ask if it was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was it published?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go on to the next document, and I think -- I just want to skip ahead a little bit, so I'm going to go to document 1D 02932. All right. Now, we see this is a document, originally it was introduced by the Prosecution. They had translated one portion of a newspaper article, and of course they left another part of the article copied on the page, so we translated it, and this relates to Dr. Haris Silajdzic, so we can sort of focus first on that document, on that part of the document, which talks about -- it says, Haris Silajdzic, Minister Of Foreign Affairs of BiH speaks for Vecernji list about the Medjurgorje agreement. Let's see what Mr. Silajdzic says.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Could I have the portion of which it refers to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you turn, it's pages -- it's not paginated.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just -- one step at a time, sir. If you look at -- it would be the fifth page, hard copy. We'll give it to you in hard copy, sir. Okay. Now you have the -- you're not going to be able to read that, but at least all you'll know exactly what I'm -- you might be able. The print is rather small. But we translated this. This portion was not translated by the Prosecution when they presented this article. He's asked a series of questions. If you look at the first question, "Minister, as a participant of the Medjurgorje talks, how do you assess the agreement reached?" His answer: "If we implement what we have agreed in Medjurgorje, that will be a successful meeting. Because, we have agreed to start implementing the Vance-Owen Plan in the liberated parts of the BiH territory. For a start, it will be implemented in Mostar, Travnik, and Zenica provinces, and I hope that the military delegations have also reached an agreement to, first of all, prevent and stop the conflicts and establish a joint command. I think that all that has been achieved." Let me stop here. Is Dr. Silajdzic correct when he says that there was an agreement to start implementing the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and when I say an agreement, an agreement between the Muslims and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was right because this confirms the text of the previous agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to spend too much more time on this because we can all read it, but let's go to the second -- to this next part, second page it would be in this printed version. He's asked a question, "Does that mean that the Medjurgorje agreement is a way to eliminate political misunderstandings and to stop the conflict between Croats and Muslims?" Answer: "If the background of these conflicts is of political nature, and it is, then it should be eliminated by virtue of disagreement, but again, I am distancing myself and say that I only believe in results." He's then asked: "Has the procedure of the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan been set up in Medjurgorje?" Answer: "Yes. One of the procedures is establishing a joint province government, and that is possible to do. The political reasons for not doing it no longer exist." Then he's asked, "How will the Medjurgorje agreement influence the future negotiations in which Serb representatives will be taking part?" Here is what Dr. Silajdzic who is the Minister of Foreign Affairs for Bosnia and Herzegovina says: "The Vance-Owen Plan must be accepted at the UN. It must become an international law. There are two signatures, Croatian and Muslim, but the Serbian one is missing. But even if we have these two signatures, they need to be implemented. One should hope that the Vance-Owen Plan will be implemented peacefully. If it cannot be done peacefully, clearly, force will be applied." Now, I'm going to stop there. To your understanding, sir, was Dr. Silajdzic, Minister of Foreign Affairs for Bosnia and Herzegovina, one of the participants of this event, was he correct in stating that both sides had agreed to the implementation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan? Are his statements correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me switch on another topic that's slightly related to this, and that concerns a goodwill mission, a delegation between the Croatian government and the Turkish government. Are you aware of such a mission and, if so, did you participate in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I did. I was a member of the Turkish-Croatian goodwill mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we can look at 1D 02726. 1D 02726. That's probably a few documents before that, the last one I read. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: 2726. Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we see that at the very top, it says 13 May 1993, and we see that this is a news conference by Croatian Foreign Minister Skrabalo. Now, at the time he would have been your boss, correct, to put it in the vernacular.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And briefly, if you could tell us, because we can all read this but if you could tell us, what was the purpose of this goodwill mission?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, to stop the conflict. Second of all, in rather general terms, to achieve a better level of cooperation between the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the one side and on the other side between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that sense, the commission wanted to tour a large part of the free territory that was not under the greater Serbian occupation. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: However, the commander of the 5th military area, General Arif Pasalic, prevented the commission's arrival at the free territory, the so-called free territory, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because we're going to go step by step. Let's not get ahead of ourselves a little bit. Let's go to the next document P 02454, and this might assist us a little bit in putting into context what you intend to tell us. P 02454. It's a P document, 2454. That probably would be the next one. We see here that there is a programme of the visit of the Mission of Goodwill to the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 19th to 22nd of May, 1993, which would have been, I guess, one day after the Medjurgorje agreement that was reached. If you could look at this document, sir, just very briefly, page through it and see whether to your understanding this was more or less the preplanned agenda for the goodwill mission between the Republic of Croatia and Turkey.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that the plan was not achieved. On the 21st and 22nd of May, we remained sitting in Mostar irrespective of the bank, whether the left or the right, and the programme did just not go through, and the reason was the fact that General Arif Pasalic prevented the goodwill mission to move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's first -- I want to go step by step, okay, because we need to make sure that there is clarity. My first question is to your understanding, was this the pre-agreed upon agenda? To your understanding.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That agenda was pre-agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now you've told us that at one part of the agenda was not materialised because of Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: He was the main instrument in preventing this programme from going through, and then the goodwill mission appointed me as the person who would go and talk to General Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you go and talk to him?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I did for over an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was it during that period of time while the delegation was in Mostar or Medjurgorje?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: We were in Medjurgorje, and I spoke with him in Mostar on the west bank, and what I achieved was for the mission to be able to cross to east Mostar, but that was the end of it. We couldn't go anywhere further from east Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During that one-hour meeting, what exactly was said? Do you recall anything significant? Do you recall anything significant that Arif Pasalic said to you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well what he told me. He told me he had received an order, that he had received an order to take Mostar and, after having taken Mostar, to move on towards the Adriatic and to take the area around Dubrovnik. I was quite shaken by that because the -- this is the territory of the Republic of Croatia. He did not manage to take the whole of Mostar despite his attempts. He wanted to go on trying. However, the effort to take the area between Mostar and the area south of Mostar all the way down to Adriatic failed through. The idea, according to him, was to establish a link which -- between the countries, the Islamic countries which were supposed to supply both arms and men, the Mujahadin, the Islamic extremists, and in that way Bosnia and Herzegovina would have gained access towards the extremist part of the Muslim world. This is something that he himself told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that you were quite taken aback. Did you report this information to anyone in particular given the content of it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we're going to get to it at some point, but are there not references to this sort of -- this conversation, what Arif Pasalic revealed to you in some of the presidential transcripts that you reviewed for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection to the leading question. If he wants to go there, then the witness should be taken to the transcripts. And may I add, Mr. President, also, I'm just looking at the revised summary of this witness's testimony that was provided to the Prosecution on Friday afternoon pursuant to the Trial Chamber's order of last week. I'm seeing here that there is a reference to Ambassador Sancevic as having participated in a Turkish-Croat mission of goodwill and his being instrumental in arranging for the medical evacuation of Bosnian Muslim soldiers there, but that's all that is said in the summary about this goodwill mission, and I think that the testimony now goes very far afield and is actually quite new and quite prejudicial - if I can put it like that - to the Prosecution in that we had no notice whatsoever that this particular aspect of the goodwill mission would be led on the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, you gave quite explicit direction as to what information, additional information you needed, and that was provided. Secondly, the information that he's just indicated, and that's why the follow-up question was -- because we will get to it. When we get to the presidential transcripts, you will see quite clearly that the gentleman makes reference of this conversation to President Tudjman during a meeting. Those presidential transcripts we got from the Prosecution. It is their documents. It behooves them to read their documents. They could have done a word search, and they would have found at some point Ambassador Sancevic revealed this conversation, and I believe it comes up in more than one occasion. So how could I have ambushed this poor Prosecutor when I'm using their documents based on all their years of investigation? They are the ones that drafted this indictment. We're here. We're answering it. I fail to see what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And if I could just add one last point, Mr. President. The practice of the parties throughout this long trial has been to give each other the courtesy of a proofing note, even over the weekend, some indication that during the proofing session additional information has come to light or will be led that falls outside the scope of either the witness statement, which of course we don't have, or the 65 ter summary. So just so you know, Mr. President, no proofing note was received throughout the weekend about this particular matter. As for the transcripts, Mr. President, we all know the volume of the materials of those transcripts, and we also know that a number of transcripts have been added by the Defence over the course of the last 72 hours as they have continued to prepare their direct examination. It's just physically impossible to know and to have instant recall of everything that's said in all of those transcripts, and it's certainly been physically impossible for to us assimilate the materials that have continued to have been added to the direct examination over the last 72 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I just -- if I may, Your Honour, because there is one incorrect piece of information that perhaps either Mr. Stringer misspoke or he certainly doesn't appreciate what exactly the Defence did. We did not introduce new presidential transcripts. What we did, what we did, we took their evidence, and we translated portions of the presidential transcripts which they refused to translate for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. I have been the one saying that all these transcripts should be translated in their entirety, but when they cherry-pick and they leave obviously, you know, the information out that is not to their favour, they can't come in later on and say, "Well, gee, I wasn't aware of that information." Presumably somebody in the Office of the Prosecution reads Croatian, and they are the ones that know exactly what sections they want to pull out. I can't read the Croatian, so, I mean, I don't see how -- I know Mr. Stringer doesn't read Croatian. Somebody in their office discriminated what was going to be translated and what was not going to be translated. Now, I suggest the better practice for him is to have his Croatian staff or B/C/S speaking staff go through the material, but it's his material, and it's not sabotage. I'm using the documents. It's fair game at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to discuss this among Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber deliberated and renders the following oral decision: The Trial Chamber, having noticed that the summaries were very succinct requested that the Prosecution and the Chamber be informed or send to the party who is developing -- who is calling the witness to develop and to present the summaries in such a way that nobody is surprised or ambushed by the questions that are going to be put. At this point, the Defence of Mr. Prlic complied to our decision, since they have sent a summary that was more elaborate than the previous summary. Upon reading this summary, it shows us that a commission, Croatian-Turkish commission was -- or met, and in the summary, it states that this commission was to talk about the issue of the evacuation of injured soldiers with the exclusion of all other topics, and this is why the Trial Chamber authorises the Prlic Defence only to raise that topic which was stated in the summary. The Prlic Defence is not allowed to raise other issues regarding the eventual involvement of the Turkish-Croatian commission when it comes to presidential transcripts regarding other topics. The Trial Chamber deems that the Prosecution, having read this summary, thought quite rightly that the witness would answer to questions on the evacuation of injured people and not on other topics. This is what I wanted to say on behalf of the Trial Chamber who deliberated. So please go ahead, Mr. Karnavas, bearing this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's look at this document, P 02454. This is the programme, sticking with this. There's one item I would like to bring to everyone's attention, and it says here, "On Friday, 21 May 1993," it says, "visits and talks in Jablanica, Prozor, Travnik, and Zenica." Did that occur?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, that did not occur. I managed to achieve General Arif Pasalic's permission to visit the eastern part of Mostar, and this is the area that we did visit. I can tell you what we saw, what we experienced in the eastern part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question. Could you please share with us what are your experiences as a result of this goodwill mission?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: When we crossed the river and reached the eastern part of Mostar, we visited people who had been in the western part of Mostar but were within the zone of General Pasalic's command. We spoke to these people, and they told us that in the eastern part of Mostar there was a number of heavily-wounded Muslims who, according to them, they did not want to go to the Croatian hospital from the western side. However, in conversation with the wounded people, we established that they did want to go there but were not allowed to go there. In addition to that, what we experienced was that when we were supposed to leave by buses from the eastern Mostar, some 30 people from eastern Mostar who were Croats and who were -- who had been beaten and ill-treated got on our buses and lied down on the bus floor and would not be convinced that we would do something for them later on so that they remained lying down on the bus floor. That's how we exited. We also spoke, as I've already mentioned, with the heavily-wounded people. When we reported about all that in Zagreb and the report was submitted by the head of the mission, Mr. Seks, what followed was a joint decision by President Tudjman and the Turkish government to do something for those heavily-wounded Muslims. I was tasked with the mission to bring them out of the city. I was in liaison with the French Battalion in order to obtain a helicopter, with the Spanish Battalion in order to obtain an APC, and also with the HVO in order to obtain their protection as we transported them to Medjurgorje, the idea being that they would be flown by helicopter from Mostar to Split, and in Split, Turkish airplanes would be waiting for them to take them to Turkey for further treatment. With this regard, I wrote a letter, the letter that you see. This is actually a plan that I drafted with a view to taking the heavily-wounded Muslims out of that war-affected area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here so we can look at this. This is P 02682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just one question to the previous document, if you allow me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sure. Which document would that be, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, this plan for the mission, do you have an idea as to what time it was drafted? The introductory paragraph mentions a visit of President Tudjman to Turkey, and it says that at that time the plan was conceived. Do you recall at what date this visit took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- or how should I put it in Croatian. After having seen the president and received the order from him, the order which he agreed upon with the Turkish government over telephone or in some other manner, everything went to Mr. Sukru Tufan who was supposed to procure the airplanes and through me; I was in charge of bringing the wounded in via Split. Both of the tasks were carried out, and over 30 Muslims were in fact flown to Turkey for treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I apologise. I can help myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. But if you could direct the witness to the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. The document is the one that we had last, the document P 02454. And it is the plan not for the evacuation of wounded persons but of the very mission, the mission of 19 to 22 May. That was obviously prepared sometime earlier. Mr. Tudjman is said to have been in Turkey for that purpose. During the official visit of Dr. Franjo Tudjman, president of the Republic of Croatia to the Republic of Turkey, this mission was conceived. The question is: Do you recall at what date that visit took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to tell you that. I was so busy with the task that I received that -- let us not forget that the plan was not achieved. The order for the evacuation of the heavily-wounded Muslims was issued after the goodwill mission. As far as the visit by President Tudjman to Turkey is concerned, I really don't know when that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Court may wish to look at 1D 02726, the one document that I had indicated which was the news conference. It is dated 13th of May. It talks about the ministers getting together. That may be of some assistance, but it may not, but at least it would seem that the ministers are getting together perhaps pursuant to what was to be arranged at a higher level. Now, if I could focus your direction on P 02682. P 02682.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you have it, sir? It says June 8th, 1993. We can see that this is from the embassy of the Republic of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's addressed to his excellency Sukru Tufan, ambassador of the Republic of Turkey in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if we look at the second page, we see that -- we see your name, and we see a signature. Sir, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, is this the letter that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This letter has to do with the plan of the evacuation of the heavily-wounded Muslims to Turkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you look at paragraph 3, now, of this letter, you say, "Security protection for wounded while in BH HVO area have been arranged with commanders B. Stojic and V. Coric." Now, first of all, I want to ask you, was -- first of all, I'm going to go step by step, so work with me. Was security protection provided?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who arranged for that? Who made the actual arrangements, you or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to Mr. Coric first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you have him here as commander. Was that your understanding that he held that position at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: No. I have to seek their pardon and that of Their Honours for having called them "commanders" because they were not commanders, and I mean military or something of that sort. This primarily had to do with police protection, and it was in that regard that Mr. Coric helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, could you please explain to us. You said "police protection." What kind of police protection was provided that was of assistance?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the column of vehicles reached Medjurgorje, the heliport in Medjurgorje, the heavily-wounded individuals were taken out of the vehicles, and we had to wait for a long while before the arrival of the French helicopters. They lay on the ground, truth be told. We did have nurses and doctors from Split who were supposed to give them a hand and be of assistance during their trip to Split. All of a sudden, onlookers, individuals who resided in the area around the heliport started gathering out of mere curiosity. It proved a useful thing to have secured and organised protection for them, and it was thanks to the police escort that I received from Mr. Coric that any sort of unpleasant incident was averted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I have to ask you for one other detail. You said that there was a meeting with Mr. Stojic. Do you recall actually recall that meeting and if so, where did it take place; when did it take place; what transpired?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Stojic, and as I indicated here, since this was a plan that I was supposed to meet with the security protection, or rather, I've put here security protection for wounded while in the BH-HVO area has been arranged with commanders B. Stojic and V. Coric. [In English] I don't remember Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You don't remember him, or you don't remember the meeting? I know we have a document here that says something, but which of the two?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] No, no. [Interpretation] I don't remember there having been a meeting with Mr. Stojic. As for Mr. Stojic himself, I do remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01520, and we're back at the goodwill mission. While we're looking for the document -- Mr. Sancevic, Ambassador Sancevic, before we get to that document, I just want to make sure that we're crystal clear. You said you knew Mr. Stojic; you don't recall the meeting. I just want to make sure, was he or was he not a commander, to your understanding, back then?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, he certainly was not a commander. I've already said that I should be pardoned for the poor terminology that I used both with regard to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at this --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: May this please be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this particular news clip, we see it's dated Medjurgorje, May 20. Again, Hina has come up, and just a couple of points because you were there. It talks about -- we see here, the very first paragraph, "The Croatian-Turkish goodwill mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina carries a message of peace not only to this part of Europe but to the entire world, stated the head of the Turkish delegation, Ambassador Mustafa Askin, at today's meeting in Medjurgorje with the mandatory for establishing a new BiH government, Dr. Jadranko Prlic." Now, is that statement correct to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it goes on to say that "The goodwill mission composed of Croatian and Turkish politicians ..." Is that correct? It was made up of politicians primarily?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, both politicians and diplomats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about where it says, "Turkey as a friend to Croatian and Bosnia and Herzegovina wishes to help in maintaining the territorial integrity of these two countries." Was that Turkey's position as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely that was the position taken by Turkey. May I say something in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: One always talks of the clashes between the Muslims and Croats. I disagree with such generalised statements. In my view, these were primarily conflicts between extreme -- extremist Muslims and extremist Croats. And if I may be allowed to say this, such a generalisation which would imply that all the Muslims and all the Croats were in conflict, that's simply untrue. Throughout 1993, there were periods where the Croats, HVO, and the Muslims, the ABiH army had excellent corporation. Let me just mention Orasije, for instance, Usora, then further down, even Zepce itself, Tuzla. It isn't fair to speak of some sort of a total, all-inclusive conflict between Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now in these documents, we see there is another reference to my client. "Dr. Jadranko Prlic welcomed the noble cause of this mission conducted in the atmosphere of Tudjman-Izetbegovic meeting." During this period of time, did you have any dealings with Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I had occasional unofficial meetings with him where -- discussed mainly the topics in which Mr. Jadranko Prlic -- at which he excelled, and these were topics related to the economy because he had a vision in what way Bosnia and Herzegovina was to be salvaged in economic terms in the future, and he had a clear vision of what had to do for the benefit of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was curious because I was a representative of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the plans and ideas that he would develop for the well-being of Bosnia-Herzegovina were something of interest to me. He was very categorical in wishing all the best for Bosnia-Herzegovina just as I did. My view of Mr. Jadranko Prlic was that of an individual who was supposed to and probably was successful in making a significant contribution to the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina in terms of the economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at document P 05051, P 05051. Just to speed it up a little bit, if we look at the last page, we see Geneva, September 14th, 1993. Do you have the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a joint declaration.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware of this joint declaration?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I was, but I was not there. I wasn't in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at paragraph number two on the second page. That would be Roman numeral I, paragraph number 2. "Provide for bilateral and unconditional disbanding of all detainee camps and for the release of detainees in territories under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and HVO immediately and by no later than September 21, 1993, at 1200 hours and bilaterally assume the responsibility for their protection and care." And then if we look at the last page, we see that there are two trustees, Dr. Mate Granic who was vice premier and minister of foreign affairs, and Dr. Haris Silajdzic, who was the minister of foreign affairs for Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, with respect to the implementation of this particular paragraph, paragraph number 2, were you involved in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there. My minister, Dr. Mate Granic, was there, and it was only logical that I should be there. The issue was the closing down of prisons, not only camps. The idea of having these prisons closed dates back as early as the 18th of May as the Medjurgorje meeting where it was mentioned for the first time and then subsequently referred to in several documents underlining the need to resolve the issue as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me get -- ask you a couple of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I see some kind of contradiction here. Actually, when our witness first said to your question answering, he said that, "I was not there. I wasn't in Geneva." It is, I believe, line 12. But later on, he said when you asked him that, were you involved in any way? Then in his answer, he said, "Yes, I was there. My minister, Dr. Mate Granic, was there, and it was only logical that I should be there." Now, it is not very clear if he's speaking about Geneva or if he speaks about the follow-up actions where, of course, he was there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was about to -- and I picked that up too, Your Honours, and I appreciate that because the there, there, it is confusing. So my follow-up question was going to be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Concretely, did you visit any detention centres because you said "there" with Dr. Granic. Is that what you're talking about and if so, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I was not present in Geneva; however, I joined Dr. Granic in touring the camps, or rather -- no, they were not camps. They were prisons which were about to be closed. I was there alongside Dr. Granic trying to provide assistance. There was also the Red Cross there and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can take a break and pick up from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed, but the Chamber would like to address Mr. Scott -- oh, no, sorry, Mr. Stringer. Mr. Stringer or Mr. Scott. It's one and the same thing. Mr. Stewart filed his submissions at 4.00 p.m. You've probably received them. Could you in ten minutes tell us about your own position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, Mr. President. I was just during the break speaking to Mr. Scott and he was -- we had received the submission from the registrar, and he's reading it as we speak, and he's going to send a message to me in the courtroom. So I think certainly at some point before the end of today we'll be in a position to inform the Trial Chamber what position, if any, we have in response to the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Karnavas, please proceed with the examination in chief of your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, and if the Court wishes to reserve the last 15 minutes for oral presentation by Mr. Stringer, we would be happy to accommodate him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador Sancevic, you indicated when we first began that you had participated in various meetings in the presence -- that were presided by the President of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, correct? That's what you told us.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I know that it's been some time, several years since the events occurred, and you were in official capacities as a Minister of Emigration and as an ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina, but could you tell us, to your best knowledge, how many times did you actually meet with Mr. Tudjman - first, that is, tete-a-tete, you know, four eyes, four ears - if you can come up with some figure and when? And then secondly, about how many times on average do you think that you met with Dr. Tudjman where he was in -- presiding over meetings? I'm not talking banquets, festivities. I'm talking actual working meetings.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I had several meetings with President Tudjman alone, tete-a-tete. There was also a number of meetings which I attended, which were of a collective nature. The meetings between President Tudjman and myself alone mainly took place in 1991 and 1992. The rest were group meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we're going to go through a set of presidential transcripts where you were present or you were mentioned, so if I could draw your attention to P 01544, 1544. It's in the second binder. Madam Usher will help you, Ambassador Sancevic. She's extremely efficient, and she'll be able to assist you. We see from the very first page that this is a VONS meeting dated 24 February 1993, and we see that you are mentioned. Where it says "With the president," we see Sancevic. Was that you, sir? Dr. S. --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. But it's not S. Sancevic but Z. Sancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it you've had an opportunity to read this presidential transcript prior to coming here today?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, time does not permit us, unfortunately, to go through all of these transcripts in great detail because if we were to do that, we'd be here for the next ten years. But at least let's focus on where you were speaking on this one, and I'm looking on the English page. It will be 21 of 52, and for you, it's -- if you look at the top right-hand side because you're looking at the Croatian, it's 01867522. Maybe if you look at the last three -- 522, the last three -- it's 01867522. The exhibit number, the exhibit number is P 01544. Okay. I understand you're going to be looking at -- Ambassador Sancevic, you will be looking at the Croatian version. That's why the different pages, okay? Now, we see your name is at the bottom of here in English. It says Dr. Zdravko Sancevic, and here you say, "During my stay in Sarajevo, I started some talks regarding these bilateral relations." Now, let me stop. This is February 24th, 1993. I assume when you're talking about -- well, by this point, had you -- you had presented your credentials to the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. It was on the 18th of December that I handed my credentials in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, by that time I was the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say here, "During my stay in Sarajevo ..." what stay are you talking about? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, I was in Sarajevo when I presented my credentials and on another two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I believe you told us that on those two occasions, you met with officials; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you go on to say, that, "However, the current situation is totally paralyzed since there was only one Croat minister of the Bosnian government in Sarajevo now ..." Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: We need to say that it concerns -- well, excuse me, let me see what the date is. It was on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't recall, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] In that precise moment [Interpretation] Excuse me. At that moment, there were not enough representatives in Sarajevo; therefore, no bilateral talks could be initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, what we're interested in is where you go on to say -- the three aspects, you say that -- above that you say, "As for my moving, the place should certainly be determined as soon as possible." And then you go on to say, "The third aspect relates to and is very important and should be dealt with particularly with regard to the president's policy of protecting people in this thing with the enclaves." And then you go on to say that "We have with the exception of three provinces where there is the free Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, we have the areas of three provinces occupied such as the west part of Bosnian Posavina and Jajce, the people who took refuge mainly in Slavonia. Then we have the Croatian enclaves in the Serbian province of Kotor Varos, Sanski Most and Ivanjska." "Then we have the Croatian enclave in the Mostar Province" -- in the Muslim province, I'm sorry -- "in the Muslim province of Usura, Komusina, Zepce, Tuzla, and Vares." Then you go on to say, "Every enclave is specific, and for every enclave we must have concrete projects about what to do in the case of escalation or attack, to avoid a repeat of the situation that took place in Derventa and Bosanski Brod." Then you say, "There we should see about the possibility of evacuation." In English, we see "exchange, return of combat units, if any, et cetera." And as I understand it, Ambassador Sancevic, having read the Croatian version, you want to make a correction to this translation where with it says "exchange." Will you please tell us what it says in Croatian. Read that sentence where it says, "There we should see about the possibility ..." Could you read that? What does it actually say?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: We can see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could just answer my question first. You had indicated --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- earlier that there needs to be a correction in that sentence, so if you could correct that first, and then I'm going to go to the next part, my next question.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] What needs to be corrected is the following: It concerned the changes that were to be introduced in terms of municipal borders. There was no exchange that was discussed in whatever derogatory sense one could understand it. It did not concern the citizens but rather the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But what did you -- what is actually on the script? Is it "exchange" or "change"? That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I object to the leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's no leading in this fashion. I've asked the gentleman to read the language and get a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you kindly please read the one sentence that I pointed out. Then we don't have objections from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will try to answer your question. It says, "promena" instead of "izmena." [In English] No is exchange, is change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're wasting time on this one issue. So please explain to us what exactly you were talking about because only you can interpret what you're saying here.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It had to do with the possibility of evacuation, changes of municipal borders, and return of combat units, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, but earlier on you're talking about three different areas. What did you mean by that? If you look at the above text that I just read, and that was the purpose of reading it. Could you please explain to us what exactly you're talking about, and why is it significant to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Enclaves in Bosnia presented a problem. There were no enclaves in the area of Herzegovina. Each enclave had its own problems. We should explore the possibility of what could take place in each of those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. We'll move on to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas. I find this interesting. You propose change -- you said you meant change of municipal borders as a solution to the problems of enclaves. Could you explain how a change of municipal borders could bring about the solution of that problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically, I will refer to Usora. Usora, with its municipal borders as they were at the time, included a number of Muslims. The majority were Croats, but there were some Muslims as well. When I had discussed the issue of Usora with Mr. Izetbegovic, he suggested that the Muslims in that municipality should be excluded or left out of the municipality, which required a change in terms of municipal borders. Changes were needed in order to keep the enclave where it was without any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if I could, picking up on that last example, if we go to the text where it says, "Every enclave is specific, and for every enclave we must have concrete projects about what to do in the case of escalation or attack, to avoid a repeat of the situation that took place in the Derventa and Bosanski Brod." Now, could you please explain to us what you meant by that? What happened in Derventa and Bosanski Brod? What took place?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: In Derventa and Bosanski Brod, what we saw was a stampede, a massive flight of civilians and then of soldiers. It was a significant defeat on the part of the Croatian Defence Council in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what attributed to this stampede? What caused it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: One reason was the way the Serbs were attacking. First, they would shell individual villages in order to drive the civilians out. Then, they would begin shelling the next village and then the village after that, which would initiate a civilian departure. After that, when the soldiers there would see the civilians leave, they would leave the front lines as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So what was the lesson to learn? How -- in your -- to your understanding, how could one go about in avoiding the repeat situation of Derventa and Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have the example of two enclaves. One was Blotinca [phoen] Slatina and the other one Usora. In Usora, the people who were from there asked me to introduce them to President Tudjman. They wanted to ask him how they were to try and fight in an enclave which is completely isolated. President Tudjman's response was, Please, do not do the same thing the Croats did in Slatina. They sent their children and their wives and families to Croatia. The only ones who were left were the soldiers. After a while, the soldiers withdrew as well. As regards Usora, he suggested that they should leave [as interpreted] and that the only ones who should be sent away were the elderly and children, of course, accompanied by the mothers and sisters. What does that mean? If a soldier does not have the possibility of leading a proper life, he cannot fight. The idea was that the enclaves could only be preserved by keeping the family structure in place, however, without the children and the elderly. To put it more plainly, the women were supposed to stay, thus enabling the soldiers to keep on fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Just a correction. On page 72, line 22, you said -- well, it's been translated that they are to -- that they should leave. As regards to Usora, he suggested that they should that they should leave. Is that what you meant to say, that they should leave, or that they should stay? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: To stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: To keep the family structure in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, just very little. Witness, can I take it from this answer that in all the examples you have made, the population that was fleeing, you referred to Croat populations; is that correct? Or did I misunderstand you? Or was it sometimes Muslims, sometimes Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Occasionally Croats, occasionally Muslims, and frequently both. For example, the flight from Jajce included Muslims and Croats together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In picking up on that, how did you know -- because you make this comment about to avoid the situation that took place in Derventa. How did you know about that? Did you read it in the newspaper? Did somebody tell you about it? Where did you get any information, if any?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: When I was appointed ambassador, President Tudjman sent me to Slavonia. By that time, I wasn't able to go any further because by that time the Serbs had occupied the area. He dispatched me there to try and establish how it was that -- well, how should I put it? How the situation came about in which the HVO had been beaten. I went there, and I talked to the people. I did ascertain why Bosanska Posavina suffered that fate. It was precisely the process I described. First, a shelling; then a massive exodus of civilians; and once they are gone, the soldiers leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now if we go to the next document, 1D 02930. This is another presidential transcript. 1D 02930, and it's dated 27 March 1993. Again, time does not permit us to go through this document in its entirety, but we notice at least in the English translation on page 32 of 37 you are featured, and I will give you the ERN number so you can look for it in Croatian. You're going to look for the following numbers: 01322427. That's in Croatian now. And you're looking at the top right-hand side. 01322427. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at that -- here you say -- you say something about receiving a call from the embassy in Rome, and you say that, "They say that there are a considerable number of young men from BH, most of them Muslim who are now escaping to Italy because it seems that their flow to Austria and Germany has somehow been stopped. So this is what they do now. They leave their documents in Istria. The documents are found, I think that your service finds the documents. They leave all the documents, and without any documents, they cross over to Italy, so a problem gradually arises there as to what to do with these people." Can you please expound on that a little bit? What was this all about, and why should the embassy be concerned because it would seem to me that this -- that's an Italian problem. They're not refugees, and let them bear the cost, so what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just like the Muslims were fleeing, leaving their documents in Italy, the same could have happened to other ethnic groups and people fleeing. The fact was that somebody had to be warned of such cases and that something needed to be done. Otherwise, the Croatian ambassador to Italy would not have called me. This meant that the Italians tabled that issue regarding those who were fleeing Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there were people fleeing Croatia, as well, Muslims or Croats fleeing Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, since you were present at the meeting, maybe you could help us a little bit. On page 26 of the English document, the English translation of this document, and we'll find it here for a second. It's page 26, and I'm referring to what Gojko Susak says and you're going to be looking for 01322421. 421 are the last three digits. 421. Because I think we can all read it and we can see what's going on between President Tudjman, Izetbegovic, Haris Silajdzic, and here we have Gojko Susak, and he's referring to a situation. If we look at -- right above it, they're referring to Konjic. Here is what Mr. Susak says: "Alija, you have five planes full of goods sitting here in Zagreb, and three are allegedly on their way. Until this is completely solved, I shall not send a single bullet."

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was present when Mr. Susak said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what does that mean? That means that the problems that the conflicts entail must be solved. How could you possibly ship weapons to someone who would then use the same weapons to attack you? I believe that there is some logic in what Mr. Susak said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next document, P 02719. P 02719. This is 11 June 1993. I'm going to be referring everybody to page 48 in particular and maybe begin by saying you weren't there but you were mentioned. You're looking for 580. Those are the last three digits, 580. Do you see where your name is? I will read it. This is Dr. Tudjman speaking to Izetbegovic. I mean, we can all read this, and I'm not going to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We will be able to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We will be able as soon as we've found it, but we're still looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. I apologise. It's 48, 48 of 75. This is in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which number is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Binder 3, the first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It's in binder 3, the first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're okay. Ambassador Sancevic, you're okay. You're okay. All right. Now, if you're looking at this document, it says here - this is Dr. Tudjman speaking, President of the Republic of Croatia - he says, "I appointed Dr. Sancevic as the ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina. He is not Herzegovinian. He is Bosnian, and as a Bosnian, he is interested in an integral Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I know he said that, but to your understanding was that one of the reasons why you were selected, or is Dr. Tudjman just saying this?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: No. There was a reason why I was appointed ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The situation in Bosnia differed from the one in Herzegovina. The Croats in Bosnia were rather mixed up with the other populations unlike the Croats in Herzegovina. Oftentimes, it is said that all of them are intermingled. No, this is not the case. Wherever you have two sides and they are intermingled, there is always a chance that one side will dominate over the other. For this reason, the enclaves in Bosnia were very important. There were no enclaves in the main area of Herceg-Bosna, and I'm referring to the area stretching along the southern Croatia. There were no enclaves there because it was a homogenous area. The same applies to the Serbs who are also in different situations in different areas and so are the Muslims. What must be distinguished is the areas where they are intermingled with others and those where they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the next document, P 03112. P 03112. This is 2 July 1993. This is a VONS meeting. Now, one could spend at least a day on this particular presidential transcript. I'm just -- my first question is -- well, we see your name here. You were present, but we do know that at times mistakes have been made. Do you -- first of all, have you read this document recently? Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And based on your reading of it, do you know whether indeed you were present at this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that I was present, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if I could just ask you for just a big general question - and I'll let others if they want to go into specifics because I don't have the time - but could you tell me, by and large, what are the discussions going on between the various parties in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina? What are they talking about? What are they referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: There were quite a few matters that they mentioned. Can you tell me more specifically what it is you want to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I guess with respect to Bosnia and Herzegovina, this is 2nd July 1993, in relation to what should happen to Bosnia and Herzegovina. To your understanding, what are the discussions about in relation to the political set-up or to its geographical make-up?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: The divisions of Bosnia and Herzegovina were discussed, and I am highly critical of that particular term "division" of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is the external division, the partition carving up, dividing on the outside. And then there is the internal division in administrative and so on and so forth. Unfortunately, in many of the documents, the gentlemen referring to this division do not distinguish between the external and internal division. The external division, that concept implies that the state is to be dissolved, divided. Now, when one refers to the internal division, that's what Vance-Owen, Cutileiro and - what's it called - the contact group were precisely referring to. What was mostly talked about was internal division, which must be distinguished from the other. Applying internal division upon the concept of the external division is to make a terrible mistake in relation to this particular term.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But in this particular document, having read it, what division are they talking about in this transcript?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: The internal division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- well, let me just ask you this question now. At times, we've heard this concept of confederation. How does that concept relate to, for instance, the internal make-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina because earlier you talked about a federation. So can you briefly tell us, what does one have to do with the other, if anything?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: There existed the idea of a confederation between a federal Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. This was one of the ideas that the Republic of Croatia put forth within the settlement-seeking process. The confederation between the republic -- the Federal Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. Evidently, this was one solution which particularly after the Washington Agreement came to the fore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, over here, we have in the transcript on page 79, line 22, it says the Federal Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you talking about the federation? You say the confederation between the republic, the federal republic -- could you please explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just find that. [In English] the confederation between the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was one solution brought about by the Washington Agreement. It was a proposition that was tabled. It wasn't just a rumour or a story that circulated. Therefore, the confederation had its significance in its own right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to go to the next document, P 06454, P 06454, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's first ask Mr. Stringer if he has any news for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I can inform the Trial Chamber now in probably 30 seconds or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We've -- sorry, Mr. President, I just had the e-mail. I haven't read the submission, but my colleague Mr. Scott has. In respect of the third sort of prayer for relief that's sought by the Petkovic Defence, who I think is the author of the submission, there's no disagreement on the part of the Prosecution, that is, that all times direct and redirect should be counted toward the total time attributable to that accused's case. It is our view that we should be -- that the Defence obviously ought to be treated in the same way that the Prosecution was such that it was not necessary to reserve in advance time that might be needed for redirect. So that's our position. In respect of the two other points raised by the submission in paragraphs -- let me -- I just misspoke. We don't agree -- I'll start over again. We do not disagree. We agree, that is to say, with paragraph 1 of the submission. We do, however, want to say that in respect of paragraphs 2 and 3 in which the Defence attempt to be seeking an assurance or a guarantee of time for redirect for every witness, we do not think that that was the case during the Prosecution case in chief. The Trial Chamber may recall the Prosecution did not always get redirect. There were times when the time was such that the Prosecution was not granted as much time as it would have liked for redirect and that essentially it boils down to a case-by-case basis or witness-by-witness basis in which the Trial Chamber should consider whether or how much time to give for redirect based upon the cross-examination. But getting back to the main point. We agree with the basic proposition that the total time is counted to the Defence, but the Defence need not reserve in advance the time that it wants for direct because that was the procedure that was applicable during the Prosecution case, and I apologise for having said all of that so inartfully and longer than 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- well, thank you for the agreement on that particular point, and obviously I understand it's not particularly easy for Mr. Stringer to be reading what his assistant has sent him by e-mail. But just in a nutshell on the observation he made about occasions on which the Prosecution did not have redirect. Essentially, what happened was that they didn't protest it because it follows from the submissions that we made in writing that if the Prosecution had simply protested and put forward the arguments we've put forward in relation to Rule 90(B), that they would and should have had the right to reexamine in every single case when they wanted to, subject to what we do say in our written submission that, of course, there's ultimate control over any examination, examination in chief, cross-examination, re-examination, if it's abusive, irrelevant and so on. But that's -- excuse me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Alaburic, who's been here throughout the trial, and I haven't, suggests that in fact the Prosecution were never quite put in the position where they wanted to do a re-examination and were actually refused or prevented from conducting a re-examination. Certainly, I do recall occasions when there's been enormous pressure at four minutes to 7.00 not to reexamine when Mr. Scott -- no doubt Mr. Scott's colleagues, as well, but I can distinctly recall Mr. Scott really protesting that he would have wanted to reexamine, but that really goes back to the point I've made that the party has a right to reexamine, and it's been a constant feature throughout this trial, the timing issue. It isn't a justification for refusing a party the opportunity of reexamining that it's, for example, four minutes to 7.00. You are entitled to reexamine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could just offer a very brief reply to that. It's my submission, Mr. President, the Prosecution did object or protest certainly when it's four minutes before 7.00, there has to be a recognition of the realities, and the realities are such that the witness in general is not going to be kept in The Hague over the course of a three or four-day weekend or longer in order to accomplish a short -- or certainly a redirect that's shorter than the examination in chief. Our submission is that rather than granting the Petkovic Defence and all of the Defence a general rule guaranteeing in every case a redirect examination, it is ultimately a matter for the discretion of the Trial Chamber, which are the situations in which a redirect is appropriate or needed in the light of the cross, and then furthermore, how much time for redirect should be granted based upon all the facts and circumstances. So it's our submission that it's a case-by-case, witness-by-witness finding that the Trial Chamber makes based on its discretion in the circumstances and that a general rule applicable to all of the witnesses who will be appearing in this court over the next months should not be granted at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I continue? Okay. If we could look at the next document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought Mr. Karnavas was going to make a -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I do --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wanted to -- no. We were dealing with a procedural issue. If you would just let me offer one sentence on the procedural issue before we go back to the witness. That seems to be the appropriate way of doing it. Just to say that if Your Honours are tempted to adopt the line that Mr. Stringer has suggested in relation to whether re-examination should be allowed at all, then I do invite Your Honours to explain very specifically in your decision, if you do take that course, why it is that Rule 90(B) does not make it actually mandatory to allow re-examination and to explain why, since Rule 90(B) refers to examination in chief, cross-examination, and re-examination, why that same approach to 90(B) wouldn't apply to cross-examination and make that also a matter of discretion of the Trial Chamber. I -- but that point is in our written submissions, but it does directly arise out of the observation that Mr. Stringer has just made, and now I will accede the floor to whoever Your Honours give the floor to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I continue, Mr. President? I know we have five minutes, but -- if we could go to the next document, P 06454. Madam -- it's there. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You need to look at page 01322934, so 934. Everyone else, it would be 44 in the English text, page 44 of 113. Have you found that, sir? Is that a yes? You're shaking your head.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go back a few pages, we'll see that you're speaking at this point uninterruptedly for several pages, which is -- okay, but the point -- my question is here, we have on page 44, you say, "As for our main body ..." Okay. Sir, you had the page. Madam Usher, if you could just assist us. Mr. Sancevic, you don't need to look through the document. The ERN number is -- the last three numbers are 934. 934. Okay. You say -- and we're going to cover this extensively tomorrow, but you say, "As for our main body, I think in the past it projected an anti-Muslim character. I believe the cause of this was Mostar and the Muslim move towards the sea and there clearly, Arif Pasalic's failure to break through towards the sea, which he had -- he personally told me this as early as when the Turkish commission came that he must have access to the sea. It is not the sea Izetbegovic talks about -- it is not the sea Izetbegovic talks about to swim in or to have a port. The sea is intended as a place where the Mujahadin from all over the world can land. That's why I think this element, we have not used it so far. Maybe for tactical reasons it was better not to mention it. But, look, they don't need to have a complete stretch from the coast up there to Konjic, although they wanted, no doubt, for this road to be secured." I would be ever so kind -- I would appreciate it if we could -- because I'm labouring under extreme stress here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you recall -- is this the incident that you were talking about when you said that you had met with Arif Pasalic and he had told you this stuff?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: This conversation took place during the first Turkish-Croatian mission because it was followed by another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what you're talking about in this transcript?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, whenever we translate something from presidential transcripts, you will see "unofficial translation." From this document, it's very clear that this part was translated by the Prosection's office. It is not a new translation. It was -- it's their document. I just wanted to point this out lest there be any incriminations as a result of trying to use guerilla tactics, which I don't believe I am using, but in any event, with that I'll have to pick it up from here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just mention? It's actually what we were discussing. I have to say that I've referred throughout to Rule 90(B), and I referred in the written submission to Rule 90(B). I don't know how, I don't know why. It's 85(B). I don't know where I got 90(B) from, the imagination or whatever, but if Your Honours would take it that in the last few days whenever I've said 90(B), I've meant 85(B). I hope that's sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to correct this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's my impression that the Trial Chamber is quite keen on ruling on this issue tomorrow morning at the beginning of the proceedings. In light of the clarification just made by counsel and in light of the fact that we've had to respond to it under these circumstances, it would be my request that the Trial Chamber perhaps allow the Prosecution, if it deems it useful, to file a very brief response to the Defence submission in a very short period of time just so that the matter could finally be joined, if you will, before the Trial Chamber rules. I think this has all happened rather suddenly and swiftly, and it might be that we would all benefit from having it addressed in a more deliberate way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can't object to that, Your Honour, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In any case, the Judges will meet tomorrow morning, very early in the morning, and we will tell you what our decision is. We will rule on this, and we will take into account what you just told us, Mr. Stringer, and we will also let you know whether you will have the authorisation to submit your filings tomorrow morning before the decision is rendered. So Witness, you are now a witness of the Court, meaning that you should not have any contacts with Mr. Prlic's attorney, but I imagine that he must have told you this when you met him. We shall reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Karnavas, I would like to tell you that you used almost 3 hours. The registrar told me that you've used up 2 hours and 58 minutes, so you will have one more hour and 22 minutes -- 1 hour and 2 minutes after the reading of the oral decision tomorrow morning. If we have no oral decision to give tomorrow morning, you will then start at 9.00 sharp. Thank you very much, and have a nice evening.
